title: Goldman Sachs: The US-China trade war is hurting economic growth
description: Futures were pointing to a lower open on Monday amid worries the trade war could push economies around the world into a recession. CNBC's Eamon Javers reports the latest on the trade war.

asr.full_text: FUTURES POINTING TO A LOWER OPEN AMID WORRIES, THE TRADE WAR COULD PUSH ECONOMIES AROUND THE WORLD INTO A RECESSION. FOR THE LATEST ON THE TRADE WAR, BAMILIA AMANJAVERS JOINS US FROM WASHINGTON. AMAN good morning. GOOLMAN SACKS COULD PUSH AT WORLD COURSE? GOOLMAN SACKS POINTED TO AN ECONOMY RECESSION. AMANJAVERS MET WITH CARELL MEEVES SOMETIMES AFTER THIS, AND ASKED WHITE LIVING FAMILY AFFORMING THE WORK OF HIGHLY PROTECTED HIGHLY RECESSION SESSIONS IN PLACE OF THE TRUTH TREADWARE, AND NOW SAYING THEY COULD PROTECT TREAT TO A HIGHLY PROTECTED HIGHLY PROTECTED ECONOMY REGULATIONS BECAUSE THE GOVERNMENT SHOWS THAT INFLATION WILL MAKE MUCH MORE THAN SOME CREATIVE INTEREST IN GOOGLE, TO FURTHER DROP IN AMERICA. I.J.'S MET WITH AN INTERESTING REPORTER WITH COPE ARTHUR, WHO ASKED ABOUT HOW TO SET OFF AN INFLATION PROCESS WITH INITIATIVES, WHERE WE CAN FIND PEOPLE WHO WANT TO MAKE MONEY MAKING AS EFFECTIVELY DELAYS. INDIVIDUAL CONSIDERED IN THE UNIVERSAL VIEW OF CENTRAL ELEMENTS, GOLDMAN SACKS putting out a note suggesting that they've concluded that the situation is a little bit worse than they thought. Here's the finding from Goldman Sachs. They're lowering their fourth quarter growth estimate to 1.8%. They called a modest change to the downside. Say that it's caused by sentiment and uncertainty. That is things like capex by companies, that might be less likely to be willing to invest in this climate. Also contributing, they say, are financial conditions and supply chain disruptions. So all of that, they say due to taking into consideration some of the uncertainty and confusion surrounding this trade situation as that trade war between the United States and China continues to grind on this week. For his part, the president over the weekend tweeting some positive sentiment himself, not offering any specifics, but just suggesting that things are going well. Progress is being made, says the president. So that's where we begin the week, Kayla. Well, Ayman, you know, it's interesting. The headlines this morning about trade worries bubbling over seem to be looking squarely at Hong Kong. And if there is military intervention there, how much more or less likely does that make Beijing's willingness to do a trade deal? We haven't heard recently from the president on Hong Kong specifically, right. He said in late July president, she was doing the right thing, but that it had been going on for a long time. Any sense of where the white house stands on this now? Well, look, the president has been taking a very light touch on the Hong Kong issue. He's been asked several times about it over the past couple of weeks. He has always sort of kept a hands-off approach on that and I think the question to look at here is what does this mean for Xi Jinping's own domestic politics? A lot of analysts will suggest that he can't afford to look weak here in the face of these protests. He also can't afford to look weak in the face of American pressure on his economy domestically. So, at some point, is there spillover from the Hong Kong situation into the trade situation or the trade situation into Hong Kong and vice versa? That's the question. This is a leader now in China who's under a lot of pressure and there's a real flash point in Hong Kong potentially brewing. So, it's something to watch. And I don't think anybody can predict with the exact certainty what's going to happen here.
